rv.q: Phillip Breen’s highly enjoyable revival at London’s Old Vic relishes the period detail, while also scoping out the shrewd social commentary and fundamental human truths that underpin the chaos.

Tying with the middle act of Michael Frayn’s Noises Off as the most ingeniously crafted and reliably hilarious half hour in English farce, it started Ayckbourn’s experiments in theatrical time and space.
Allam delivers a masterclass in comic timing.
The world of Ayckbourn's play is an odd one to visit.
It’s a reminder that this genius writer delivers his comedy with a sting in the tail.
But it also feels overlong and occasionally laborious, the comic engine taking time to grind into gear and the broadly drawn characters sometimes grating, for all the energy of their embodiment here.
It’s also wildly implausible and dated.
Luckily, Ayckbourn prescribes a restorative cure with this invigorating evening's entertainment.
With choreographic precision, Phillip Breen’s ingenious direction makes the most of Ayckbourn’s witty, inventive script.
A deliciously amusing exposure of class anxiety and gender politics, it is as relevant today as it was when written in 1969.
To achieve the feat with an ease and ordinariness which belies the effort, demonstrates both the skill and wit of both the writer and the players assembled to deliver his lines.
Philip Breen's direction ticks like clockwork, slyly hints at their class duality.
A groan-worthy sitcom full of innuendo, a farcical comedy of manners and the absurd.
Say only that it’s delivered with perfectionist energy and the streak of sad humanity behind the jokes that is a perennial mark of Ayckbourn.
Philip Breen’s direction works wonders with Ayckbourn’s script that has us watching two couples living their parallel lives at the same time, overlapping in a real-life Venn diagram.
This comedy has so many great lines in it, there is plenty to laugh at.
How the Other Half Loves contains an undeniably clever theatrical idea at its heart, but this revival struggles to overcome the age of the material.

cn.t: Ayckbourn's 1969 farce earns mostly warm reviews for its clever construction and Roger Allam's masterful comic performance, though some find the comedy contrived and dated despite its still-relevant themes of class and gender politics.
